title: The Louisiana Purchase
text:
In 1802 the United States learned that Spain had secretly returned the vast Louisiana territory to France and that Spanish officials had closed New Orleans to American trade. Farmers west of the Appalachians shipped their goods down the Mississippi through that port. President Thomas Jefferson sent Robert Livingston and then James Monroe to Paris to try to buy New Orleans and some land on the river.

Napoleon's plans had changed. His army sent to retake Saint-Domingue, the base for a new French empire in America, had been destroyed by the Haitian revolution and yellow fever. War with Britain was about to resume, and Louisiana could not be defended. In April 1803, to Livingston's astonishment, the French minister offered to sell not just New Orleans but all of Louisiana.

The American envoys had no authority for such a purchase, but they did not let the chance pass. They agreed to a price of 60 million francs plus the assumption of certain claims, about 15 million dollars in total. The treaty, dated 30 April 1803, roughly doubled the size of the United States. Livingston is reported to have said that it was the noblest work of their whole lives.

Jefferson had doubts about whether the Constitution allowed such an acquisition, but he set them aside, and the Senate approved the treaty that autumn.
lesson: Pay attention to the other side's situation, not just your own request. When they need to sell, a much larger deal may be possible than the one you came for.
people: Thomas Jefferson, Robert Livingston, James Monroe, Napoleon Bonaparte, Talleyrand, Francois Barbe-Marbois
source: Treaty between the United States and the French Republic (1803); diplomatic correspondence of Livingston and Monroe
